1 Pendubot notebook technical notes

A step by step companion to the standalone DDP and iLQR notebook

These notes explain how the robot model becomes a working optimal controller. Read them beside the notebook, moving between the named section and its code cell. The central result is a torque sequence that swings the robot from hanging downward to upright. Trajectory feedback corrects deviations during swing-up, and a separate local LQR controller holds the robot upright afterward.

The current notebook contains 24 executable code cells. DDP and iLQR have separate Hamiltonian functions, backward passes, complete solvers, and run cells. They use the same robot, objective, initial guess, and nonlinear forward simulation, so their numerical results can be compared.

How to use the explanations

Each topic starts with the physical or mathematical reason for the calculation, then connects it to a function or a short excerpt copied from the notebook. Equation numbers belong to these notes; notebook section references identify where the matching code is located. Code is shown selectively to make its purpose clear; the notebook remains the complete executable implementation.

The saved reference run converged for both methods to J approximately 5.17531. This measured result is explained later rather than treated as a value that every changed experiment must reproduce. The mechanics now follow the supplied four-page derivation, with intermediate signs reconciled explicitly. These notes were prepared on 24 November 2026.

2 Running the notebook in the correct order

Notebook sections 1 and 2 and the separate run cells in section 14

A notebook remembers variables and functions in its active Python kernel. A code cell uses definitions made by earlier cells. If cells are run out of order, a result may depend on an older parameter value or may fail because a name has not been defined. For a clean starting point, select Kernel, then Restart Kernel and Run All Cells.

Installation and first execution

Install the packages in requirements.txt in a Python environment, open the notebook in JupyterLab or VS Code, and select that environment as the kernel. The repository README gives the Windows and Ubuntu commands. No dashboard, project Python module, or downloaded data is required.

JAX compiles several functions the first time they are used. A pause during compilation is expected. Saved plots are reference outputs from an actual execution; rerunning replaces them with results from the current settings. The inline animation is intended to run inside Jupyter.

Where to make a parameter change

cfg = Config()
# Put a change immediately after the line above:
cfg = replace(cfg, m2=1.2, duration=8.0)

Config is immutable because it is a frozen dataclass. replace creates a new configuration with selected fields changed. Assign the result to cfg; writing replace(cfg, m2=1.2) by itself creates a value but does not update the configuration used below. Rerun from section 2 onward.

3 Coordinates and the passive elbow

Notebook section 2 and joint_positions

A Pendubot has two rotating links but only one motor. The first joint is attached to the base motor; the elbow is passive. The motor can still influence the elbow because the two bodies exchange forces through their connection. That coupling appears explicitly in the mass matrix.

(3.1)

q1 is measured from the downward vertical. With the drawing axes, increasing q1 moves the first link toward positive horizontal position. q2 is the relative elbow rotation, so the absolute orientation of link 2 is q1 + q2. It is not measured from the fixed vertical independently.

(3.2)

At the initial state both links hang down at rest. At the target both links are extended upward at rest. The zero second torque means there is no elbow actuator; it does not mean the elbow angle or elbow acceleration must remain zero. Angles used in all calculations are in radians.

4 Parameters and useful physical quantities

Notebook section 2 and coefficients

Symbol or fieldDefaultMeaning
m1 and m21 kg eachMass of each uniform rod
l1 and l21 m eachTotal length of each rod
gravity9.81 m/s^2Gravitational acceleration
dt0.02 sControl sampling interval
duration6 sSwing-up planning horizon
n300Number of control intervals
q(1, 1, 0.1, 0.1)Running weights in state order
q_terminal(2000, 2000, 200, 200)Terminal weights in state order

The centre of mass of a uniform rod lies halfway along it. Its rotational inertia about its centre is m l^2 / 12. These assumptions determine the inertial coefficients; they are not separate tuning parameters in this notebook.

(4.1)

Changing a mass changes inertia and gravity. Changing a length changes the centre-of-mass location, moment of inertia, gravity leverage, and coupling. A longer or heavier link therefore changes several terms together. Editing only a displayed coefficient would break that consistency.

The horizon must contain an integer number of sampling intervals. For example, 6 / 0.02 = 300. The notebook checks positive masses, lengths, timing, gravity, and torque penalty, as well as the length and sign of the weight tuples. cfg is passed explicitly to model and controller functions.

5 Centre of mass positions from the supplied derivation

PDF page 1 and notebook sections 2 and 3

Use the same notation as the supplied handwritten derivation. P1 and P2 are the centre-of-mass position vectors, r1 and r2 are distances measured along the links, and qs is the absolute angle of link 2. Upward Y is positive. The default rods have unit mass and unit length, with their centres halfway along each link.

(5.1)
(5.2)
(5.3)

For l1 = l2 = 1 m, the first centre is [one half sin(q1), minus one half cos(q1)]. The second is [sin(q1) plus one half sin(qs), minus cos(q1) minus one half cos(qs)]. These are the same two position vectors written on page 1 of the PDF.

def com_positions(x, cfg):
    q1, q2 = x[:2]
    r1, r2 = cfg.l1/2, cfg.l2/2
    qs = q1+q2
    P1 = jnp.array([r1*jnp.sin(q1), -r1*jnp.cos(q1)])
    P2 = jnp.array([cfg.l1*jnp.sin(q1)+r2*jnp.sin(qs),
                    -cfg.l1*jnp.cos(q1)-r2*jnp.cos(qs)])
    return P1, P2

The function returns two length-two vectors. Their second entries are the heights used in gravitational potential energy. The tip is not P2: P2 lies halfway along link 2, while the animation tip is at its end. This distinction prevents treating the full link length as a centre-of-mass distance.

6 Differentiating positions and squaring speeds

PDF page 1 and com_velocities

Differentiate the horizontal and vertical components separately. The derivative of sin(qs) includes the chain-rule multiplier qs dot = v1 + v2. Speed is the Euclidean length of the velocity vector, so speed squared is the sum of the squared components; adding the components before squaring would introduce a false cross term.

(6.1)
def com_velocities(x, cfg):
    q1, q2, v1, v2 = x
    r1, r2 = cfg.l1/2, cfg.l2/2
    qs, vs = q1+q2, v1+v2
    dP1 = jnp.array([r1*jnp.cos(q1)*v1, r1*jnp.sin(q1)*v1])
    dP2 = jnp.array([cfg.l1*jnp.cos(q1)*v1+r2*jnp.cos(qs)*vs,
                     cfg.l1*jnp.sin(q1)*v1+r2*jnp.sin(qs)*vs])
    return dP1, dP2

With the default unit lengths, squaring dP1 gives one quarter times v1 squared. For dP2, the cross terms contain cos(q1) cos(qs) plus sin(q1) sin(qs). The cosine difference identity reduces this factor to cos(qs - q1) = cos(q2).

(6.2)
(6.3)

The handwritten velocity-component lines should be read as vector components before taking the norm. The later squared-speed expansion in the PDF supplies the correct scalar expression. The notebook now follows that component-by-component calculation directly.

7 Adding the two link kinetic energies

PDF page 2 and kinetic_energy

Each rod contributes translation of its centre of mass and rotation about that centre. The absolute angular speeds are omega1 = v1 and omega2 = qs dot. For unit rods, I1 = I2 = 1/12 kg m^2. Use these values together with the squared speeds derived on the previous page.

(7.1)
(7.2)

Add T1 and T2, then replace qs dot by v1 + v2 and collect the three velocity products. This reproduces the boxed kinetic energy on page 2 of the PDF.

(7.3)
def kinetic_energy(x, cfg):
    dP1, dP2 = com_velocities(x, cfg)
    I1, I2 = cfg.m1*cfg.l1**2/12, cfg.m2*cfg.l2**2/12
    v1, v2 = x[2:]
    T1 = 0.5*cfg.m1*(dP1@dP1)+0.5*I1*v1**2
    T2 = 0.5*cfg.m2*(dP2@dP2)+0.5*I2*(v1+v2)**2
    return T1+T2

The code keeps the two physical contributions visible instead of defining kinetic energy through the mass matrix. That makes the later energy-based Euler-Lagrange check independent of the manually assembled inertia entries. Edited masses and lengths still work because the same geometric calculation uses cfg.

8 Potential energy and the Euler Lagrange convention

PDF pages 1 and 2 and potential_energy

Use U for gravitational potential energy, as in the supplied derivation. Lowercase u remains the base motor torque. Each gravitational energy is mass times gravity times upward centre-of-mass height.

(8.1)
(8.2)
def potential_energy(x, cfg):
    P1, P2 = com_positions(x, cfg)
    return cfg.m1*cfg.gravity*P1[1]+cfg.m2*cfg.gravity*P2[1]

Use the sign convention on PDF page 2

(8.3)

The isolated L = U - T line on page 1 is reversed relative to the later derivation. Page 2 uses L = T - U and obtains the correct final motion equations. The notebook and these notes consistently follow that convention with the applied torque on the right.

(8.4)
(8.5)

The second form follows because U is independent of velocity. The base has tau1 = u, and the passive elbow has tau2 = 0. Defining the Lagrangian packages the energies; Euler-Lagrange is the additional mechanical law used to obtain the motion.

9 Deriving the first joint row with numerical coefficients

PDF page 2 and notebook section 4

Start from the boxed default kinetic energy. Differentiate with respect to v1, holding the coordinates and v2 fixed. The factor two from differentiating v1 squared turns 5/6 plus one half cos(q2) into 5/3 plus cos(q2).

(9.1)

Take the time derivative with the product rule. A coefficient containing cos(q2) contributes minus sin(q2) times v2 as it changes along the motion.

(9.2)
(9.3)

Substitute into d(Tv1)/dt - Tq1 + Uq1 = u. Both gravity terms are positive on the left of the mechanical equation. The velocity terms are negative in this row.

(9.4)

The mixed acceleration coefficient is the inertial coupling. It explains why the base motor cannot be modeled as moving only link 1. Every term in this row has torque units.

10 Deriving the passive joint row and its cancellation

PDF page 2 and notebook section 4

(10.1)

When differentiating the coefficient of v1, keep the one half multiplying cos(q2). The correct mixed term in the time derivative is minus one half sin(q2) v1 v2. One intermediate handwritten line omits this factor, but the final cancellation and row on the PDF use the consistent result.

(10.2)
(10.3)

Now subtract Tq2. Its mixed term becomes positive and exactly cancels the negative mixed term in the time derivative. Write the unsimplified row to see that cancellation.

(10.4)
(10.5)

The right-hand side is zero because the elbow has no motor. It can still accelerate through its inertial coupling with the base and the remaining gravity and velocity terms.

11 Assembling the supplied M C and G expressions

PDF page 3 and notebook sections 3 to 5

(11.1)
EntryDefault expressionMeaning
M115/3 + cos(q2)First diagonal inertia
M12 = M211/3 + (1/2) cos(q2)Symmetric inertial coupling
M221/3Second diagonal inertia
C1-sin(q2) (v1 v2 + (1/2) v2^2)First velocity term
C2(1/2) sin(q2) v1^2Second velocity term
G114.715 sin(q1) + 4.905 sin(qs)First gravity term
G24.905 sin(qs)Second gravity term

Capital C in your PDF is a two-component vector, not a 2 by 2 matrix multiplying velocity. The function name remains coriolis_gravity, but its returned velocity vector is explicitly named C. At the hanging state M = [[8/3, 5/6], [5/6, 1/3]], while C and G are zero.

def coriolis_gravity(x, cfg):
    q1, q2, v1, v2 = x
    _, b, _, alpha, beta = coefficients(cfg)
    C = jnp.array([-2*b*jnp.sin(q2)*(v1*v2+0.5*v2*v2),
                    b*jnp.sin(q2)*v1*v1])
    qs = q1+q2
    g2 = beta*jnp.sin(qs)
    G = jnp.array([alpha*jnp.sin(q1)+g2, g2])
    return C, G

For edited physical parameters, b = m2 l1 r2, alpha = (m1 r1 + m2 l1)g, and beta = m2 r2 g. The defaults give b = 1/2, alpha = 14.715, and beta = 4.905. The compact earlier coefficients a = 5/3 and d = 1/3 give exactly the same mass entries.

12 Residual torques and the two row equations

PDF page 3 and notebook section 5

Move the velocity and gravity vectors to the right. This is a change of side in the same mechanical equation, not a new model. Name the two remaining generalized torques r1 and r2, as on page 3 of the PDF.

(12.1)
(12.2)
(12.3)

Keep both gravity signs negative in r1

The PDF has a plus sign before the last gravity contribution in one expanded residual line. Its earlier G vector places both terms positively on the left. Subtracting that vector therefore gives the two minus signs shown above. The code implements [u, 0] - C - G directly, avoiding that transcription error.

The symbol r is reused in the handwritten pages

On page 1, r1 and r2 mean centre-of-mass distances in metres. On page 3, they mean residual torques in N m. These uses are separate contexts. The notebook keeps the local geometry radii inside the geometry functions and names the torque vector residual inside dynamics. The unrelated configuration field cfg.r is the control-effort weight.

(12.4)
(12.5)

These are exactly the two scalar rows of M times acceleration equals residual torque. The first two state derivatives are already known: x1 dot = v1 and x2 dot = v2. The remaining task is to solve these rows for the two accelerations.

13 Eliminating accelerations and constructing the state model

PDF pages 3 and 4 and dynamics

Subtract M12 times row R2 from M22 times row R1. The second acceleration cancels. For the other acceleration, follow page 4 and subtract M11 times R2 from M21 times R1. Use symmetry M21 = M12.

(13.1)
(13.2)

The first second-acceleration fraction is the form boxed in the PDF. The second is the form used in the code. Their numerators and denominators differ by the same minus sign, so they are identical. A positive common determinant keeps both code expressions consistent.

(13.3)
def dynamics(x, u, cfg):
    M = mass_matrix(x[:2], cfg)
    C, G = coriolis_gravity(x, cfg)
    torque = jnp.ravel(jnp.asarray(u))[0]
    residual = jnp.array([torque, 0.0])-C-G
    determinant = M[0, 0]*M[1, 1]-M[0, 1]**2
    acceleration = jnp.array([
        M[1, 1]*residual[0]-M[0, 1]*residual[1],
        -M[0, 1]*residual[0]+M[0, 0]*residual[1]])/determinant
    return jnp.concatenate((x[2:], acceleration))

At the hanging state with the default rods, Delta = 7/36. A base torque of 1 N m produces accelerations [12/7, -30/7] rad/s^2. This makes the state derivative [0, 0, 12/7, -30/7], demonstrating again that zero elbow torque does not imply zero elbow acceleration.

14 Reconciliation of the handwritten intermediate lines

How the supplied derivation is used and checked

The final coupled equations in the supplied PDF agree with this implementation. The following clarifications keep the intermediate steps consistent with those final equations.

PDF locationClarification used here
Page 1 LagrangianUse L = T - U from page 2, with tau on the right of Euler-Lagrange.
Page 1 velocitiesDifferentiate position components, then use speed squared = dX^2 + dY^2.
Page 2 derivative of Tv2Keep the factor 1/2 in - (1/2) sin(q2) v1 v2.
Page 3 expanded r1Subtract both gravity contributions because residual = [u, 0] - C - G.
Page 4 q2 accelerationThe negative denominator is valid; negate numerator and denominator to get the code form.

Independent checks against the supplied formulas

Notebook section 7 transcribes the default M, C, and G directly into paper_default_terms using NumPy. At 25 deterministic test states, it compares the resulting linear solve with the general dynamics function. It also checks the boxed kinetic energy and the signed-denominator acceleration formula.

The energy-based Euler-Lagrange residual now differentiates T computed from physical centre-of-mass velocities, rather than T computed from the same manually assembled mass matrix. This gives an additional independent connection between the geometric derivation and the implemented mechanical rows.

The notebook remains self-contained: the source PDF is not needed at runtime. The mechanics derived here supply the common RK4 model for the separate DDP and iLQR implementations that follow.

15 Predicting one step with RK4

Notebook section 6 and rk4 and rollout

The continuous model tells us the instantaneous rate of change. The optimizer instead needs the state after one sample interval. RK4 estimates that next state by evaluating the derivative at the start, twice near the midpoint, and once near the end. The torque stays constant during that interval.

(15.1)
(15.2)
def rk4(x, u, dt, cfg):
    s1 = dynamics(x, u, cfg)
    s2 = dynamics(x+dt*s1/2, u, cfg)
    s3 = dynamics(x+dt*s2/2, u, cfg)
    s4 = dynamics(x+dt*s3, u, cfg)
    return x+dt*(s1+2*s2+2*s3+s4)/6

The weighted average is an approximation to integrating the derivative over the interval. RK4 is a fourth-order method for sufficiently smooth dynamics, but it is not exact. A smaller step generally improves accuracy at the cost of more calculations.

@partial(jax.jit, static_argnames=("cfg",))
def rollout(u, x0, cfg):
    def body(x, uk):
        xn = rk4(x, uk, cfg.dt, cfg)
        return xn, xn
    _, xs = jax.lax.scan(body, x0, u)
    return jnp.concatenate((x0[None], xs))

scan carries the current state into the next step. Each step returns the next state twice: once as the new carry and once as an item to store. The final concatenation restores the initial state, giving N+1 state samples for N control intervals. With the defaults, u is (300, 1) and x is (301, 4). The column dimension of u is retained for matrix-compatible control formulas.

16 Checking that the mechanical implementation is consistent

Notebook section 7 and the printed model checks

Model checks answer specific questions before optimization is attempted. A controller can reduce a cost computed from incorrect equations, so a falling objective alone does not verify the physical model. The notebook checks energy, equilibrium, and independent Euler-Lagrange residuals.

CheckHow it is computedSaved result
Positive inertiaSmallest eigenvalue over 101 elbow angles0.0662791
Mechanical residualDifferentiate energy and substitute dynamics1.77636e-15 N m
Energy drift at dtMaximum unforced energy change over 2 s5.24542e-6 J
Energy drift at dt/2Repeat with half the step1.92821e-7 J

The independent Euler Lagrange check

The code defines the Lagrangian directly from the geometric energy functions and differentiates it with JAX. Its velocity derivative is generalized momentum. The Jacobian of this momentum times the state derivative is its time derivative by the chain rule. Subtracting the coordinate derivative and applied torque should leave approximately zero.

(16.1)
(16.2)

How to interpret a small nonzero number

Floating-point arithmetic does not represent most real numbers exactly. A residual around 10^-15 in this calculation is consistent with rounding, whereas a residual around 1 would suggest a sign, indexing, or modeling error. Double precision is enabled before constructing the JAX arrays.

At zero torque both the hanging and upright states have zero acceleration, although upright is unstable without feedback. In an unforced frictionless simulation, total energy should remain constant; the small drift comes from numerical integration. The lower drift after halving dt supports the integration check for this tested trajectory.

The additional PDF-specific checks compare 25 deterministic states: maximum acceleration error 6.03961e-14, kinetic-energy error 4.44089e-16, and difference between second-acceleration denominator forms 6.39488e-14.

17 Defining the optimization problem

Notebook section 8 and objective

The decision variables are the N base torques. Once those torques and the initial state are known, rollout determines every predicted state. The optimizer seeks a torque sequence that balances state error and effort while arriving close to the upright target.

(17.1)
(17.2)

The dt factor makes the running sum approximate a continuous-time integral. It is not applied to the terminal term, which is a penalty at one time. The factor one half makes derivatives of quadratic forms simpler. Q and QN are diagonal matrices created from the two state-weight tuples.

@partial(jax.jit, static_argnames=("cfg",))
def objective(x, u, cfg):
    Q, QN = cost_matrices(cfg)
    e = x-GOAL
    running = cfg.dt/2*(jnp.einsum("ni,ij,nj->", e[:-1], Q, e[:-1])+cfg.r*jnp.sum(u*u))
    return running+0.5*e[-1] @ QN @ e[-1]

e[:-1] includes state samples 0 through N-1 for the running cost. e[-1] is the terminal error. einsum sums the quadratic state cost over all running samples. sum(u*u) sums the squared base torques. The result is a scalar used to accept or reject every proposed trajectory.

Why the cost does not wrap angles

The specified target is the numerical angle pi, not every equivalent orientation. A quadratic unwrapped error preserves that choice and is smooth. Physical reporting later wraps angles to compare equivalent orientations. These are distinct tasks. A terminal penalty encourages arrival but is not a hard equality constraint, and a torque penalty is not a hard torque limit.

18 How weights and the initial guess influence the solution

Notebook sections 2 and 8

ChoiceWhat it encouragesWhat to examine
Larger running position weightsSpend more of the horizon near the targetApproach time and effort
Larger terminal weightsReduce the final state errorArrival error and convergence
Larger rUse less torquePeak torque and missed-target tradeoff
Longer durationAllow more maneuvering timeTrajectory shape and computation
Different initial_uStart the local search elsewhereStatus and final cost

With diagonal weights, the four state contributions follow the fixed order q1, q2, v1, v2. A value of 2000 in the first terminal entry therefore penalizes terminal base-angle error, while 200 in the third entry penalizes terminal base-speed error. The weights also absorb the different physical units of angle, speed, and torque in the designer's scalar objective.

(18.1)

For example, a terminal base-angle error of 0.1 rad by itself contributes one half times 2000 times 0.1 squared, which equals 10. A terminal base-speed error of 0.1 rad/s contributes 1 with the default third terminal weight. These calculations show what the chosen weights mean.

initial_u = jnp.asarray(
    4*np.sin(np.pi*np.arange(cfg.n)*cfg.dt)
)[:, None]

This deterministic sine-wave guess has amplitude 4 N m and period 2 s. The optimizer is not restricted to sinusoidal torques; it changes each sample independently. DDP and iLQR receive the same array. Because this is nonlinear local optimization, changing the initial guess may alter the iteration count, the local solution, or whether a usable solution is found.

19 Derivatives of the discrete model

Notebook section 9 and trajectory_jacobians and trajectory_hessians

The backward pass needs to know how the next state changes if the current state or torque changes. Pack all five inputs into z = [q1, q2, v1, v2, u]. Differentiate the complete RK4 map F, including its intermediate stages, so the derivatives match the numerical model being optimized.

(19.1)
(19.2)
@partial(jax.jit, static_argnames=("cfg",))
def trajectory_jacobians(z, cfg):
    packed = lambda zi: rk4(zi[:4], zi[4:], cfg.dt, cfg)
    return jax.vmap(jax.jacfwd(packed))(z)
@partial(jax.jit, static_argnames=("cfg",))
def trajectory_hessians(z, cfg):
    packed = lambda zi: rk4(zi[:4], zi[4:], cfg.dt, cfg)
    return jax.vmap(jax.jacfwd(jax.jacrev(packed)))(z)

jacfwd constructs a Jacobian with forward automatic differentiation. Combining jacfwd and jacrev constructs the output Hessians. vmap applies that calculation at every trajectory sample. jit compiles the batched calculation. None of these operations uses finite differences to generate the derivatives used by the optimizer.

The notebook separately checks them with centred finite differences. The saved maximum errors are about 8.77e-12 for the Jacobian and 4.86e-10 for the Hessian. Those comparisons test derivative implementation at the selected probe; they do not prove accuracy at every possible state.

The tensor axis order matters

The first Hessian axis selects a next-state component. The final two axes select inputs in z. Thus Fzz[:, :4, :4] contains state-state curvature and Fzz[:, 4:, :4] contains input-state curvature. Interchanging an output axis with an input axis would give the wrong Hamiltonian terms.

20 Bellman value and the local Hamiltonian

Notebook section 10 before the separate method cells

Imagine that the cost of completing the maneuver from the next state were already known. For the current step, choose a torque by adding the immediate cost to that future cost. Bellman's principle expresses this idea through the value function V: the best remaining cost from a state.

(20.1)
(20.2)

The notebook calls the expression inside the minimization a discrete local Hamiltonian. It is also often called an action-value function. Its units are those of the objective. It is not the mechanical energy and not the continuous-time Pontryagin expression involving a costate times the continuous dynamics.

Distinguish potential energy from future objective cost

U in the mechanics chapter denotes gravitational potential energy. Plain V in the control chapter denotes future objective cost. The derivatives Vx and Vxx are the gradient and Hessian of that future cost with respect to state.

(20.3)

We cannot generally write the full nonlinear value function in closed form. DDP and iLQR instead carry a local quadratic approximation along a nominal trajectory. A bar over x or u means the current nominal value, and delta means a proposed small deviation from it.

(20.4)

The backward pass computes the coefficients of this quadratic, minimizes it with respect to the torque deviation, and passes a new local value approximation to the previous stage.

21 Deriving the Hamiltonian gradients

Notebook sections 10a and 10b

Use the chain rule on H = running cost plus next-stage value evaluated at F. A change in the current state first changes F through A, then changes the future value through Vx. A change in torque follows the same path through B.

(21.1)

For a one-input robot, Hx is a four-component column and Hu is a one-component column. The transpose of A maps a next-state value gradient back to a current-state gradient. The transpose of B maps it back to a torque gradient.

(21.2)
Q, _ = cost_matrices(cfg)
A, B = Fz[:, :4], Fz[:, 4:]
Hx = cfg.dt*Q@(x-GOAL)+A.T@Vx
Hu = cfg.dt*cfg.r*u+B.T@Vx

This excerpt is present in both Hamiltonian functions. The direct running-state gradient would encourage reducing current error. The A-transpose Vx contribution also considers how the current state affects later cost. The torque gradient similarly combines immediate effort and future consequences.

Why the gradients agree but the methods can differ

At a fixed nominal trajectory and with the same supplied value derivatives, both methods use these first-derivative formulas. They differ in the second-derivative formulas on the next pages. Once their backward recursions evolve, their value approximations and trajectories may also differ, so matching gradient formulas does not imply identical optimization paths.

22 Full DDP keeps dynamics curvature

Notebook section 10a and hamiltonian_blocks_ddp

Differentiate A transpose Vx once more. There are two effects: Vx changes through F, producing A transpose Vxx A; and A itself changes with the current inputs, producing the second derivatives of F weighted by Vx. Full DDP retains both effects.

(22.1)
(22.2)
(22.3)
def hamiltonian_blocks_ddp(x, u, Fz, Fzz, Vx, Vxx, cfg):
    Q, _ = cost_matrices(cfg)
    A, B = Fz[:, :4], Fz[:, 4:]
    Hx = cfg.dt*Q@(x-GOAL)+A.T@Vx
    Hu = cfg.dt*cfg.r*u+B.T@Vx
    curvature = jnp.einsum("i,ijk->jk", Vx, Fzz)
    Hxx = cfg.dt*Q+A.T@Vxx@A+curvature[:4, :4]
    Hux = B.T@Vxx@A+curvature[4:, :4]
    Huu = cfg.dt*cfg.r+(B.T@Vxx@B)[0, 0]+curvature[4, 4]
    return Hx, Hu, Hxx, Hux, Huu

curvature is a 5 by 5 matrix. The expression einsum("i,ijk->jk", Vx, Fzz) sums over the four output-state components and leaves the two input axes. curvature[:4, :4] is the state-state block, curvature[4:, :4] is the torque-state block, and curvature[4, 4] is the scalar torque block.

There is only one input, so Huu is stored as a scalar for efficient division later. Hux has shape (1, 4). The code's Hamiltonian check differentiates a scalar composed value expression directly and confirms that its gradient and Hessian match these block formulas.

23 iLQR drops only the dynamics curvature terms

Notebook section 10b and hamiltonian_blocks_ilqr

iLQR approximates deviations in the next state using only A delta x + B delta u. It still uses the true nonlinear F for nominal and trial rollouts. With this local linear approximation, the second derivatives of the dynamics do not appear in the local quadratic cost.

(23.1)
(23.2)
def hamiltonian_blocks_ilqr(x, u, Fz, Vx, Vxx, cfg):
    Q, _ = cost_matrices(cfg)
    A, B = Fz[:, :4], Fz[:, 4:]
    Hx = cfg.dt*Q@(x-GOAL)+A.T@Vx
    Hu = cfg.dt*cfg.r*u+B.T@Vx
    Hxx = cfg.dt*Q+A.T@Vxx@A
    Hux = B.T@Vxx@A
    Huu = cfg.dt*cfg.r+(B.T@Vxx@B)[0, 0]
    return Hx, Hu, Hxx, Hux, Huu

This function has no Fzz argument and no tensor contraction. It is a separate implementation, not a call to the DDP function with a hidden method switch. The check in section 10b differentiates the scalar local Hamiltonian built from linearized dynamics, which is the approximation iLQR uses.

FeatureFull DDPiLQR
First derivatives of FRequiredRequired
Second derivatives of FRequiredNot evaluated by its solver
Value Hessian VxxRetainedRetained
Forward simulationNonlinear RK4Nonlinear RK4
Search and objectiveShared definitionsShared definitions

Omitting dynamics curvature reduces derivative work, but does not establish that iLQR will always take fewer iterations or find a better solution. Which local model is more useful depends on the problem, initialization, regularization, and numerical implementation.

24 Finding the torque correction and feedback gain

Notebook section 11 and the sign convention for k and K

Once the local Hamiltonian is quadratic, find its minimizing torque deviation by setting its torque derivative to zero. For a fixed state deviation, the terms depending on torque are Hu transpose delta u, delta u transpose Hux delta x, and one half delta u transpose Huu delta u.

(24.1)

If Huu is positive, the local quadratic curves upward in torque and the stationary point is a minimum. Full DDP can produce nonpositive curvature away from a solution. The implementation adds a nonnegative scalar mu so the control minimization is well posed.

(24.2)
(24.3)

k is the feedforward correction: what to change even if the state equals the nominal state. K is feedback: how to alter the torque when the state deviates. The code defines k and K with positive inverse formulas, so the control policy contains minus signs. Mixing this convention with gains that already contain a minus sign would reverse the update.

regularized = Huu+mu
ok = jnp.isfinite(regularized) & (regularized > 1e-10)
denominator = jnp.where(ok, regularized, 1.0)
k, K = Hu/denominator, Hux/denominator

A one input numerical example

Suppose Huu = 2, mu = 0.5, Hu = 1, and Hux = [0.5, 0, 0, 0]. Then k = 0.4 and K = [0.2, 0, 0, 0]. For delta x = [0.1, 0, 0, 0], the full local correction is -0.42 N m. At the nominal state it is -0.4 N m. This example illustrates the algebra, not a saved robot sample.

25 Passing the value approximation backward

Notebook section 11 and the value recursion

After choosing the local policy, substitute delta u = -k - K delta x into the original quadratic Hamiltonian. Collect terms linear and quadratic in delta x. The constant term affects the approximate value but is not needed for the gradient and Hessian recursion used here.

(25.1)
(25.2)

For example, substituting into one half delta u transpose Huu delta u produces a linear term delta x transpose K transpose Huu k and a quadratic term one half delta x transpose K transpose Huu K delta x. The mixed Hamiltonian term supplies the two negative cross terms in Vxx.

new_Vx = Hx-K.T@Hu-Hux.T@k+(K.T@k)*Huu
new_Vxx = Hxx-K.T@Hux-Hux.T@K+(K.T@K)*Huu
new_Vxx = (new_Vxx+new_Vxx.T)/2

The gains were computed using regularized Huu + mu, but this substitution uses the original Huu. That is the convention implemented by both notebook methods. Replacing all appearances of Huu in the recursion with the regularized number would define a different local value update.

Start at the terminal cost

(25.3)

At the last state there are no remaining control intervals, so the future value is exactly the terminal penalty. Compute these derivatives, then move through stages N-1, N-2, down to 0. The backward pass is a recursion because each stage needs the value derivatives from the next.

A true Hessian is symmetric. Averaging a matrix with its transpose removes small numerical asymmetry before using it at the previous stage. This is a numerical consistency operation, not an additional state penalty.

26 Reading the two backward pass implementations

Notebook sections 11a and 11b

Full DDP backward pass

@partial(jax.jit, static_argnames=("cfg",))
def backward_pass_ddp(x, u, jac, hess, mu, cfg):
    _, QN = cost_matrices(cfg)
    terminal = (QN@(x[-1]-GOAL), QN, jnp.array(True))

    def body(carry, data):
        Vx, Vxx, valid = carry
        xi, ui, Fz, Fzz = data
        Hx, Hu, Hxx, Hux, Huu = hamiltonian_blocks_ddp(xi, ui, Fz, Fzz, Vx, Vxx, cfg)
        regularized = Huu+mu
        ok = jnp.isfinite(regularized) & (regularized > 1e-10)

The incoming carry contains next-stage Vx, next-stage Vxx, and a validity flag. Each time sample supplies a nominal state, nominal torque, Jacobian, and dynamics Hessian. The DDP Hamiltonian function computes the full local model. The remaining body computes the gains and value update shown on the previous two pages.

iLQR backward pass

@partial(jax.jit, static_argnames=("cfg",))
def backward_pass_ilqr(x, u, jac, mu, cfg):
    _, QN = cost_matrices(cfg)
    terminal = (QN@(x[-1]-GOAL), QN, jnp.array(True))

    def body(carry, data):
        Vx, Vxx, valid = carry
        xi, ui, Fz = data
        Hx, Hu, Hxx, Hux, Huu = hamiltonian_blocks_ilqr(xi, ui, Fz, Vx, Vxx, cfg)
        regularized = Huu+mu
        ok = jnp.isfinite(regularized) & (regularized > 1e-10)

The iLQR version accepts no dynamics Hessian. Its sample data contain only the state, torque, and Jacobian, and it calls the iLQR Hamiltonian function. The remaining regularization, sign convention, terminal values, and value recursion are the same algebra.

How scan handles backward time

(_, _, valid), (ks, gains) = jax.lax.scan(
    body, terminal, (x[:-1], u, jac, hess), reverse=True)
return ks, gains, valid

This last excerpt is the DDP scan; iLQR omits hess from the sample tuple. reverse=True evaluates the recurrence from the final interval backward. The stored arrays are returned in chronological order, so index k still means the gain for forward time step k. The accumulated validity flag rejects unusable control curvature or nonfinite value derivatives.

27 Testing the policy on the nonlinear robot

Notebook section 12 and forward_pass

The local model describes only a neighborhood of the nominal trajectory. Its proposed correction must therefore be tested on the actual nonlinear RK4 model, starting again at the original initial state. This forward pass produces a complete candidate state and torque sequence.

(27.1)
@partial(jax.jit, static_argnames=("cfg",))
def forward_pass(x, u, ks, gains, eta, cfg):
    def body(xnew, data):
        xb, ub, k, K = data
        unew = ub-eta*k-K@(xnew-xb)
        xn = rk4(xnew, unew, cfg.dt, cfg)
        return xn, (xn, unew)
    _, (xs, us) = jax.lax.scan(body, x[0], (x[:-1], u, ks, gains))
    return jnp.concatenate((x[:1], xs)), us

xb and ub are the old nominal state and torque. xnew is the candidate state reached so far in this rollout. The feedback term corrects the departure of that new state from the nominal state. It is active even while optimizing, before the final controller is executed.

Line search and regularization have different jobs

The outer solver tests eta values 1, 1/2, 1/4, down to 1/128. Only the feedforward term is scaled by eta in this implementation. The feedback gain remains unchanged during a trial. A candidate is accepted only if its evaluated objective is finite and strictly smaller than before.

If none of the candidate step sizes works, the solver increases mu and recomputes the backward pass. Mu changes the computed gains, while eta tests how far to move along a particular correction. After an accepted step, mu is divided by three, down to a small lower bound. Rejected candidates never replace the nominal trajectory or appear as accepted convergence points.

28 Following the complete DDP solver

Notebook section 13a and solve_ddp

The separate DDP solver makes every method-specific operation visible. First it reshapes the supplied guess to (N, 1), rolls out the states, and evaluates the starting cost. It rejects a nonfinite initial trajectory before attempting a backward pass.

def solve_ddp(initial_u, cfg):
    started = time.perf_counter()
    u = jnp.asarray(initial_u, dtype=jnp.float64).reshape(cfg.n, 1)
    x = rollout(u, X0, cfg)
    J = float(objective(x, u, cfg))
    if not np.isfinite(J):
        raise ValueError("Initial trajectory is not finite; change the guess or time step.")
    costs, records = [J], []
    mu, status = 1e-3, "iteration_limit"

    for iteration in range(cfg.max_iterations):
        z = jnp.concatenate((x[:-1], u), axis=1)
        jac = trajectory_jacobians(z, cfg)
        hess = trajectory_hessians(z, cfg)
        accepted = False
        for retry in range(16):

Within each outer iteration, z combines each running state and its torque. DDP evaluates both derivative orders. The inner retry loop calls the DDP backward pass using the current mu. For a valid pass, the solver records the maximum absolute feedforward correction and tries candidate forward step sizes until one reduces the objective.

After a candidate is accepted

(28.1)

The solver records the new cost, relative decrease rho, correction size, step size, and mu. It then replaces x and u with the accepted candidate and reduces mu. Ordinary convergence requires both a small relative decrease and a small maximum feedforward correction; either one alone is insufficient. The defaults are rho below 1e-8 and correction below 1e-3 N m.

Why the final backward pass matters

The gains used to propose the last accepted step were computed around the previous nominal trajectory. After the loop, DDP reevaluates Jacobians and dynamics Hessians at the final trajectory and recomputes feedback gains. That prevents execution from using stale gains. It increases a small gain regularization if needed and raises an error if no finite final gain set can be found.

29 Following the complete iLQR solver

Notebook section 13b and solve_ilqr

The iLQR solver is a separate function and a separate notebook cell. Its initialization and cost accounting match DDP, but its loop evaluates only the first derivatives of F. There is no zero-filled substitute tensor and no call to the DDP solver hidden inside this method.

def solve_ilqr(initial_u, cfg):
    started = time.perf_counter()
    u = jnp.asarray(initial_u, dtype=jnp.float64).reshape(cfg.n, 1)
    x = rollout(u, X0, cfg)
    J = float(objective(x, u, cfg))
    if not np.isfinite(J):
        raise ValueError("Initial trajectory is not finite; change the guess or time step.")
    costs, records = [J], []
    mu, status = 1e-3, "iteration_limit"

    for iteration in range(cfg.max_iterations):
        z = jnp.concatenate((x[:-1], u), axis=1)
        jac = trajectory_jacobians(z, cfg)
        accepted = False
        for retry in range(16):
            ks, gains, valid = backward_pass_ilqr(x, u, jac, mu, cfg)

The method-specific call is backward_pass_ilqr(x, u, jac, mu, cfg). It creates gains from the local linear-dynamics approximation. The same nonlinear forward_pass then evaluates proposed torques, and the same objective judges whether a candidate is useful.

StageDDP solveriLQR solver
Trajectory derivativesJacobians and dynamics HessiansJacobians only
Backward callbackward_pass_ddpbackward_pass_ilqr
Candidate simulationforward_pass with nonlinear RK4forward_pass with nonlinear RK4
Cost acceptanceFinite and lower objectiveFinite and lower objective
Final gainsRecompute using full DDP curvatureRecompute using iLQR approximation

Why the separate code is useful for learning

Read the two loops side by side after understanding the shared forward pass. The placement of the derivative calculations shows where DDP spends additional work. The gain and value formulas show exactly how those derivatives influence its update. The independent run cells make it easy to rerun one method while retaining the other result for comparison.

30 Understanding returned results and stopping status

Notebook sections 13 and 14

Result fieldShape or typeHow to use it
x(N+1, 4)Nominal joint states including the initial state
u(N, 1)Optimized base torques
gains(N, 1, 4)Trajectory feedback matrices
costScalarFinal objective
costsAccepted count + 1Initial objective followed by accepted objectives
historyList of recordsCost decrease, correction, step size, and mu
statusTextReason the optimization loop stopped
secondsScalarMeasured solver time after shared warmup
gain_regularizationScalarRegularization for final feedback gains

The status is evidence about the numerical search

converged means both ordinary stopping tolerances were met after an accepted step. stationary means no decreasing step was found with a small correction at low regularization. iteration_limit means the outer iteration budget was exhausted. line_search_failed means the allowed retry process ended without an accepted step and without the stationary condition.

A solver can reach a physically useful state without satisfying very tight optimization tolerances. It can also stop with a small numerical update while retaining an unacceptable arrival error. Therefore inspect the status, final objective, and measured physical errors together.

ddp_result = solve_ddp(initial_u, cfg)    # Section 14b
ilqr_result = solve_ilqr(initial_u, cfg)  # Section 14c
# Run section 14d afterward to refresh the comparison.

Both functions receive the same initial_u; the optimized output of one is not passed to the other. Timing is a single measured run on this computer after explicit shared kernel warmup, not a hardware-independent speed guarantee.

32 Reading the state and torque trajectories

Notebook section 15 and joint state ordering

The first angle approaches pi while the relative elbow angle returns to zero. The passive elbow initially folds in the negative direction, and both links later become aligned upright. The velocity curves show motion during the maneuver and decay toward rest.

The torque curve is a held value over each sample interval, so it is drawn as a step plot. It is the base motor torque only; there is no second control curve because the elbow has no actuator. A peak near 27 N m is allowed because the notebook has an effort penalty but no hard actuator saturation constraint.

The selected result is the lower-cost run. Very small cost differences can select DDP or iLQR without implying a meaningful physical difference in the plotted maneuver.

33 Trajectory feedback and the upright LQR controller

Notebook section 16 and upright_lqr

The optimized torque sequence is a plan. Open-loop execution simply replays it. Trajectory feedback also observes the current state and corrects its difference from the nominal planned state, using the final gains returned by the optimizer.

(33.1)

At the end of swing-up both execution policies switch to a separate local LQR controller. Linearize the discrete RK4 model at the upright target and zero torque. The local state error approximately follows e next = Astar e + Bstar u.

(33.2)
(33.3)
(33.4)
def upright_lqr(cfg):
    z = jnp.concatenate((GOAL, jnp.zeros(1)))
    Fz = np.asarray(trajectory_jacobians(z[None], cfg)[0])
    A, B = Fz[:, :4], Fz[:, 4:]
    QL, RL = cfg.dt*np.diag([100., 100., 10., 10.]), cfg.dt*np.array([[.1]])
    P = solve_discrete_are(A, B, QL, RL)
    K = np.linalg.solve(RL+B.T@P@B, B.T@P@A)
    radius = np.max(np.abs(np.linalg.eigvals(A-B@K)))
    return K, radius

SciPy solves the discrete algebraic Riccati equation for P. np.linalg.solve computes the gain without explicitly forming the inverse shown in the mathematical formula. The maximum absolute closed-loop eigenvalue is about 0.94655 in the saved run. Being below one supports local linear stability near upright, not guaranteed capture from an arbitrary distant state.

34 Executing with finer integration and interpreting failures

Notebook section 16 and execute and fine_step

Planning uses one RK4 step per control interval. Execution uses ten RK4 substeps while holding the chosen torque constant over that interval. The controller still updates every dt; this is a more accurate plant integration, not a tenfold faster feedback controller.

@partial(jax.jit, static_argnames=("cfg",))
def fine_step(x, u, cfg):
    return jax.lax.fori_loop(0, 10, lambda _, state: rk4(state, u, cfg.dt/10, cfg), x)

Even the nominal open-loop experiment starts with a small numerical-model mismatch because planning and execution use different integration accuracy. The unstable robot amplifies that difference. An initial angle offset adds another mismatch. The open-loop trials fail to arrive near upright and terminate numerically shortly after the LQR switching time.

The local LQR cannot be assumed to recover from the large state errors left by failed open-loop swing-up. Trajectory feedback keeps the two tested runs close to the plan and brings them into the upright neighborhood where the local holding controller is useful.

35 Success criteria and performance measurements

Notebook section 16 and physical_error

For physical reporting, equivalent angles should describe the same orientation. The helper subtracts the target and wraps each angle difference into the interval from -pi up to pi. Velocity errors are not wrapped. This helper is not used by the optimization objective.

def physical_error(x):
    error = np.array(x, dtype=float)-np.asarray(GOAL)
    error[..., :2] = (error[..., :2]+np.pi) % (2*np.pi)-np.pi
    return error
MeasurementCriterionWhen evaluated
Arrival angleEach absolute angle error below 0.05 radAt the swing-up horizon
Arrival speedEach absolute speed error below 0.10 rad/sAt the swing-up horizon
Hold angleEach absolute angle error below 0.10 radOver the full extra 5 s
Hold speedEach absolute speed error below 0.25 rad/sOver the full extra 5 s

The feedback run passes only if it satisfies the relevant angle and speed conditions. The execution table also reports whether the full simulation completed and, if not, the time at which a nonfinite state or a state magnitude above 1e5 triggered a numerical stop.

36 Understanding the animation code

Notebook section 17 and joint_positions

The animation draws joint positions from the executed nominal feedback run. It does not solve a new optimization problem or change the controller. Understanding this separation helps when a displayed motion looks unexpected: first inspect the stored states and their units.

def joint_positions(x, cfg):
    q1, q2 = np.asarray(x)[:2]
    elbow = np.array([cfg.l1*np.sin(q1), -cfg.l1*np.cos(q1)])
    tip = elbow + np.array([cfg.l2*np.sin(q1+q2), -cfg.l2*np.cos(q1+q2)])
    return np.array([[0.0, 0.0], elbow, tip])

The elbow is one first-link length from the origin. The tip is one second-link length from the elbow using the sum q1 + q2. The negative cosine in the vertical coordinate makes zero angle point downward, matching the mechanical derivation.

How a frame is made

For each displayed sample, update_animation computes three points: base, elbow, and tip. It updates the two plotted line segments and the time label. The phase label changes from trajectory feedback to upright LQR at the horizon. The base remains fixed at the origin.

A stride selects roughly one displayed frame per 0.10 s for the default sample time. Skipping display frames reduces the embedded animation size; it does not skip simulation or feedback updates. FuncAnimation creates the frame sequence, and to_jshtml embeds it for Jupyter playback.

If the animation does not appear on GitHub

The notebook file stores HTML for playback, but GitHub does not execute notebook JavaScript as a Jupyter kernel would. Open the notebook in JupyterLab or VS Code and run the animation cell. The convergence and trajectory figures remain useful static results even without animation.

39 Troubleshooting and short understanding checks

Use the model status and outputs to locate the issue

A name is not defined or a plot shows an older result

Restart the kernel and run all cells. If you intentionally run only one method again, first confirm that the common setup and its function definitions have run, then refresh section 14d and the plots. Changing cfg without rerunning later cells leaves earlier arrays unchanged.

The optimizer reaches its iteration limit

Read the final physical errors and the convergence curve. If the cost is still decreasing, a larger budget may help, but check the horizon, initial guess, and integration step as well. Do not relabel the result as converged merely because a plot looks close to the target.

The open loop trial fails even with no initial offset

Planning and execution use different integration resolution. Small discrepancies can grow in unstable motion, especially near upright. The nominal feedback trial is the relevant comparison for seeing whether trajectory feedback corrects that tested discrepancy.

Questions with worked answers

1. Why can q2 accelerate if its torque is zero? The second motion equation includes the base acceleration through M12, along with velocity and gravity terms. With default parameters at the hanging state and a base torque of 1 N m, q2 acceleration is -30/7 rad/s^2.

2. Does iLQR simulate a linear robot? No. It uses linearized deviations in its backward local model and the nonlinear RK4 map in every forward rollout. Its function has no dynamics Hessian input.

3. If k = 0.4, K delta x = 0.02, and eta = 0.5, what is the torque change? The implemented policy gives -eta k - K delta x = -0.22 N m. Only the feedforward term is scaled by eta.

4. If an iteration reduces cost by 1e-10 relative to the old cost but the feedforward correction is 0.1 N m, is ordinary convergence satisfied? No. The small relative reduction condition passes, but 0.1 is larger than the 1e-3 N m correction tolerance.

5. Is a low nominal objective enough to prove robust execution? No. Check the trajectory feedback execution, arrival criteria, full hold interval, and completion flag under the conditions actually tested. The notebook does not establish global stability or robustness to arbitrary errors.
